conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your little one has arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the **EPDS** (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s just 10 gentle questions about your mood, thoughts, and experiences over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, everything stays confidential, and we can pause or slow down whenever you need. Ready to start?

In the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Patient: Most days I’ve still been able to laugh—maybe not as easily as before the baby, but when my partner makes a silly face or when the dog does something goofy, I catch myself giggling. It’s not every single moment, but I’d say I’ve laughed pretty normally at least half the time.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Patient: Yeah, I’ve been able to laugh—like, yesterday my little one let out a burp that startled both of us, and I burst out laughing. It hasn’t disappeared completely, it’s just… maybe a beat slower than usual.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Patient: I still catch myself looking forward to little things—like my morning coffee once the baby’s down for a nap, or the short walk we usually take around the block in the evening. It’s not this big burst of excitement, more like a quiet “oh, that’ll be nice,” but it’s there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Patient: Not really. I mean, if the baby’s fussy I’ll wonder for a second if I missed a cue, but it’s more curiosity than blame. I don’t sit there beating myself up—mostly I just move on to the next thing that might help.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Patient: Sometimes I’ll get a sudden “what if the baby’s too hot or too cold?” or “did I sanitize that bottle well enough?”—little flashes that pop up out of nowhere. They’re quick, though; I check on him, decide everything looks fine, and the worry drifts off. It’s not all day or anything, just a couple of random moments.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Patient: I haven’t had that panicky, heart-racing feeling. I get a little startled when he makes a weird newborn noise in the night—like every new mom probably does—but it’s not real fear. I calm down as soon as I peek in the bassinet and see his chest moving up and down.
Things have been getting on top of me

Patient: A couple of times, sure—like yesterday when the laundry pile looked taller than me and he wouldn’t settle in the swing. For maybe ten minutes I thought, “How am I going to do all this?” But I took a breath, folded two onesies, and it felt manageable again.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Patient: No, sleeping’s actually one thing that’s going okay. Once I’m out, I’m out—his stretches are getting longer, so most nights I get a decent chunk. I haven’t lain there feeling miserable or wired, thank goodness.
I have felt sad or miserable

Patient: I wouldn’t call it miserable—more like quick little waves of “ugh, today feels long.” They pass in minutes, especially if I step outside or cuddle him close. I still smile every day, so it’s not this heavy sadness hanging around.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Patient: I really haven’t cried much at all. Maybe one teary moment last week when I couldn’t get him to latch right away, but it was short. No sitting around sobbing or anything like that.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
Patient: No, never. I want to be here for my baby, not hurt myself. That kind of thought hasn’t crossed my mind.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 7: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item EPDS-style questionnaire, self-report (≤ 2 wk postpartum)

Symptoms endorsed  
• Transient, mild low mood (“quick waves of ‘ugh, today feels long’”) – resolves within minutes  
• Occasional intrusive worries about infant safety (temperature, bottle sanitation) – brief, no avoidance or compulsions  
• Brief sense of being overwhelmed (e.g., laundry/settling episodes) – self-resolves with simple coping

Symptoms denied  
✓ Persistent anhedonia – still laughs & anticipates small pleasures  
✓ Excessive guilt / self-blame – only fleeting curiosity about infant cues  
✓ Panic spells, nocturnal mood-related insomnia, crying spells, suicidal/harm ideation

Pattern summary  
No evidence of sustained depressive or anxiety symptoms meeting clinical threshold. Emotional shifts are situation-specific, short-lived, and do not impair basic functioning or bonding. Negative cognitive content, vegetative symptoms, and safety concerns absent.

Screening impression  
Current risk for major postpartum depression or anxiety disorder: LOW. Continue routine postpartum follow-up; educate on normative emotional changes, stress management, and red-flag symptoms; re-screen at 6-wk visit or sooner if clinical change.
